title: Valid and Invalid Argument Forms
short: Modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical and disjunctive syllogism are valid forms; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid.
trouble: Affirming the consequent looks like modus ponens. Check which part of the conditional the second premise matches.

blocks.html: Some argument patterns are so common that they have names. You met them in words in The Two Conditional Fallacies; now truth tables (Validity by Truth Table) prove which are valid and which are not.

head: Name
Form
Valid?
blocks.cap: Four valid forms and two look-alikes.

blocks.html: A form is valid when every argument of that shape is valid, whatever statements the letters stand for. To name an argument's form, check which part of the conditional the second premise matches: the antecedent or the consequent, affirmed or denied.

Validity depends only on form. In modus ponens, the only row with $p \to q$ and $p$ both T has $q$ T, so there is no counterexample, and that stays true whatever $p$ and $q$ mean. Affirming the consequent has a counterexample row ($p$ F, $q$ T), so some argument of that shape has true premises and a false conclusion. That is why we can call the whole form invalid.

blocks.title: Name the form
blocks.q: "If the oven is hot, the bread bakes. The bread did not bake. So the oven is not hot."
steps: The second premise denies the consequent.

blocks.title: A look-alike
blocks.q: "If you study, you pass the quiz. You passed. So you studied."
steps: The second premise affirms the consequent, not the antecedent.
You might have passed for another reason.

blocks.a: Modus tollens, with formulas in place of the letters.

blocks.title: Disjunctive syllogism in words
blocks.q: "Either the key is in the drawer or it is in my coat. It is not in the drawer. So it is in my coat."
steps: The first premise is a disjunction.
The second denies one disjunct; the conclusion is the other.

blocks.html: Each named form covers infinitely many arguments, because the letters can stand for any statements, simple or compound. Spotting the form under bigger parts, as in the third example, is the skill that natural deduction will use on every line.

Confusing affirming the consequent with modus ponens, because both have a conditional and a plain second premise. Point to the second premise and ask which side of the arrow it matches. Matching the antecedent gives modus ponens; matching the consequent is the fallacy.
